about.title: Where I come from and where I'm headed
paragraphs: I'm a Systems Engineer graduated from Universidad Nacional de Costa Rica, with a diploma in Application Programming. My path started in full stack development, but from early on I was more drawn to the question of what to do with the data that software ends up producing.

I formalized that curiosity by working with Python, Pandas, and Tableau on personal sports analytics projects, while still building real production systems. I did my professional internships at Grupo Eulalia, where I built a work order module in React for a truck repair workshop, and at Ticotek, where I designed the database schema and API for a shipment control system.

Right now I'm actively looking for work as a Data Analyst or Business Intelligence Analyst in Costa Rica, without leaving full stack development behind. I don't see myself moving from one field to the other. I'm comfortable working in both: understanding a business need, building the system that solves it, and then sitting down with that data to explain what's happening and why.

barca.title: FC Barcelona: what explains the successful seasons?
barca.question: What better explains FC Barcelona's successful seasons: transfer spending, coaching decisions, or factors like squad market value and academy player usage?
barca.finding: Transfer spending and academy usage don't explain performance in a statistically significant way. What does explain it is coaching continuity and squad market value.
context: I analyzed 33 FC Barcelona seasons (1993/94 through 2025/26) using real data I collected and cross-checked by hand wherever automated coverage wasn't reliable, not a generic dataset pulled without review.

I split the analysis by coaching era (Guardiola, post-Messi, Xavi, Flick) because mixing such different periods dilutes the real patterns: what explains a successful season under one playing style doesn't necessarily hold under another.

I was careful not to confuse correlation with causation. A year with a bigger transfer budget can be a result of the club already being in a good financial and sporting position, not the spending itself causing the following success.
barca.methodology: I cross-referenced five variables (net transfer spending, coaching changes, minutes played by La Masía academy players, squad market value, and coaching continuity) against each season's performance, using Pearson correlation and ANOVA to separate what's statistically significant from what only looks like a trend.
dataSources: datahub.io — historical LaLiga results going back to the 1993-94 season
FBref — possession and xG per season, extracted with BeautifulSoup and Pandas
Kaggle and manual compilation — transfer spending and squad value, with cross-validation wherever automated coverage wasn't reliable
barca.limitations: Some seasons have weaker data coverage than others, especially in the 90s, and a few are outliers due to off-field context (institutional crises, board changes) that no statistical variable captures well. I'd rather state that explicitly than let the analysis look more certain than it is.

messi.title: Messi: the statistically unrepeatable at World Cups
messi.statusNote: This project doesn't have any data collected or a dashboard yet. What you're seeing here is the full outline; the analysis and visuals come next.
messi.question: Is there a historical World Cup player who comes close to the simultaneous combination of excellence across functional roles that are normally mutually exclusive, or is Messi a true statistical outlier?
messi.thesisTitle: The important precision behind this thesis
thesis: The point of this analysis isn't that Messi is the number one in every individual category. In fact, he isn't: Mbappé ended up with more total World Cup goals than him after 2026.

The actual point is different: football demands roles that require almost mutually exclusive skill sets, and what's statistically abnormal isn't winning a single category, it's showing up in the top range (top 3-5) of several different functional roles at the same time.
messi.rolesTitle: The four functional roles being compared
messi.rolesIntro: Functional roles, not nominal positions on the pitch, since the same player shifts position over the course of a career.

roles.name: Finisher
roles.description: Converts chances into goals: goals, xG, shot conversion, shots on target.

roles.name: Unbalancer
roles.description: Creates individual danger by taking on defenders: successful dribbles, fouls drawn, progressive carries.

roles.name: Playmaker (the final pass)
roles.description: Creates the direct chance: assists, key passes, xA, big chances created.

roles.name: Deep-lying orchestrator
roles.description: Circulates the ball and progresses the attack from deeper zones: progressive passes, pass completion rate, passes into the final third.

messi.comparisonPlayers: Cristiano Ronaldo, Neymar, Mbappé, Ronaldinho, and Maradona (still need to confirm whether the same level of statistical detail is available for the 1986 World Cup).
dataSources: SofaScore — event-level stats documented back to the 1966 World Cup, no official API
FBref — reliable advanced metrics from the 2018 World Cup onward
Kaggle — base goal data per match and per World Cup
messi.note: The idea that this means Messi is "underrated" is my own personal reflection, not a conclusion that follows directly from the data. I'm presenting it separately from the objective findings of the analysis.

pulperia.title: Store credit system for a family grocery store
pulperia.statusNote: The app is finished and in active use. The only thing missing is the screenshot session with sensitive data masked out, so this section is intentionally incomplete for now.
problem: My family's corner store kept track of "fiado" (informal customer credit) in a paper notebook, with everything that implies: illegible handwriting, lost pages, no way to audit who wrote what or when, and no backup if the notebook got damaged or lost.
I built this app to replace that notebook with a system the store staff could use just as naturally as they used paper, but with real traceability and access from any device.
features: Real-time updates with Firebase Realtime Database: multiple people can log sales and payments at the same time and see updates instantly on every device.
Full traceability: nothing gets deleted, every record keeps track of who created or edited it and when.
PIN-based profiles: several family members share one login, but every action stays tied to a specific person.
Receipt printing formatted for an 80mm thermal printer, with an option to share the receipt over WhatsApp.
Automatic WhatsApp alerts to the customer on every transaction, using a dedicated number for the store.
pulperia.screenshotsPlaceholder: This is where 3-4 screenshots of the real usage flow will go: the main view with the customer list, logging a sale or payment, the receipt or WhatsApp notification, and the PIN-based profile system. Names, phone numbers, and profile photos will be blurred before publishing; amounts without an attached name aren't sensitive.
pulperia.stack: React and Vite on the front end, Firebase (Realtime Database and Authentication) as the backend, deployed on Vercel with continuous deployment from GitHub. All the infrastructure runs on each service's free tier.
